summary: Readable as a 1100 L four-castor Eurobin, but it is a smooth grey box with a soft pillow lid, no hardware and no wear.
critique: The proportions are about right: roughly 1.26 x 1.0 x 1.37 m, tapered body, four castors, side trunnions. The construction is what gives it away. The body is one smooth, flat-shaded slab with no galvanised character: no swaged horizontal stiffening ribs, no rolled top rim, no vertical corner pressings. The lid is a thick rounded pillow (about 150 mm deep, fully filleted) that sits on a thin band. Real Eurobin lids are either a thin flat or domed HDPE moulding with a moulded lip and two front handles, or a galvanised flat lid, and they hang on a visible hinge bar at the back. The trunnions are plain cylinders with no backing plates or end flanges. In the side view, the two 'buttons' on the front face read as eyes and do not correspond to a real feature. The castors are tiny, about 100 mm, and attach straight to the underside. Real Eurobins use 200 mm castors on swivel plates bolted under a welded base frame, with a brake pedal on two of them. There is no drop-front or bottom drain plug, no council or ID stencil, no dents, no rust, no grime. The material is a uniform mid-grey with mid roughness and no metallic response, so the body reads as plastic rather than galvanised steel.
suggestions: Lid: replace the pillow with a 40-60 mm thick moulded lid with an 80 mm down-turned lip, a slight dome (20-30 mm), two moulded hand grips on the front edge, and a rear hinge bar (a 25 mm tube running the full width, with 3-4 knuckles). About 400 tris.

Body: add a rolled top rim (a 30 mm torus-section bead around the opening), two horizontal swaged ribs about 300 mm apart on all four faces (inset 8-10 mm), and vertical chamfered corners. About 300 tris. Alternatively, bake these into a normal map.

Base and castors: add a welded angle-iron base frame (40 mm) inset under the body, 200 mm castors with swivel forks and top plates, and a brake pedal on the two front castors. About 600 tris per bin at LOD0.

Trunnions: make them 50 mm diameter x 100 mm, on a 150 x 150 mm welded backing plate with an end flange, mounted at about 2/3 height on the 1000 mm sides. Remove the two front 'buttons', or replace them with a drain plug at the bottom of the front face.

Material: galvanised body should be metallic 1.0, albedo about 0.55-0.6 linear grey, roughness 0.45-0.65 with spangle and blotch variation from a 512 tiling mask. Add grime streaks running down from the rim, scuffs on the lower 300 mm, a white stencil number decal, and an optional coloured lid variant (green, blue, black HDPE, roughness 0.6). One shared 1K atlas.
Add small dents and a slight lid misalignment as per-instance variation so that rows of bins don't look identical.
renderer_notes: Flat ambient makes the dark lid and the shadowed side faces read almost black. Some of the flatness is the lack of GI, but the absence of surface detail is the asset's problem.

summary: Correct 40 ft proportions and corrugated walls, but clean, unbranded and missing the corner castings, door hardware and wear that make a container read as real.
critique: The overall size looks right (12.19 x 2.44 x 2.59 m), and the side corrugation profile is there and catches the light. Everything else is what an untextured blockout would show. The corner castings are tiny dark specks, where real ones are 178 x 162 x 118 mm boxes with oval apertures that clearly break the silhouette at all eight corners. The corner posts and top and bottom side rails don't read as separate members. The roof is perfectly flat; real roofs have shallow transverse corrugations or panel dents. The door end shows faint vertical lines but no four locking bars with cam keepers, handles, hinges or door gasket frame. The front (blind) end should have its own corrugated panel inside a visible frame. There is no CSC plate, no owner code or BIC number (e.g. ABCU 123456 7 with 45G1 size code), no logo, no rust bleeding from the rails, no scrapes or dents. The paint is a single flat mid-blue that looks like satin plastic rather than weathered marine paint, and the darker side vs lighter end values come only from lighting. It also sits directly on the ground: real ones rest on their bottom corner castings, which leaves a 0-30 mm gap and dark under-shadow along the floor cross-members.
suggestions: Corner castings: add 8 boxes (178 x 162 x 118 mm) with an oval 'hole' (a dark decal or a small inset) on each exposed face, in raw dark grey-rust steel. Make the corner posts 150 x 150 mm L-sections visibly proud of the corrugated panel by about 20 mm. About 200 tris total.

Door end: model 4 vertical locking bars (Ø 27 mm tube, full height) with top and bottom cam keepers, 4 handles at about 1.1 m height, 6 hinge blocks per door edge, and an inset door panel frame. Use a shallow 3-flute corrugation on the doors. About 1.2k tris; the far end can be a normal-mapped quad for LODs.

Rails: add top and bottom side rails as separate box sections (top 60 x 100 mm, bottom rail 160 mm deep C-section), plus a forklift-pocket-free bottom edge with visible cross-member ends every 300 mm (normal map or small tris).
Roof: add a shallow transverse corrugation or 5-6 slight dents with a normal map, plus rust-stained puddle marks.

Materials: use a 2K trim sheet shared across all container colours. Base paint albedo variations (Maersk blue, rust red, grey, green), roughness 0.5-0.7. Add rust bleed from the rails and corner castings, scrape marks exposing primer and rust along the bottom rail, and chalk or paint repair patches in a mismatched shade.

Decals: owner code and serial with check digit on the doors and top-right of the sides, a 45G1 size code, a CSC plate on the left door, a large company logo on the sides, and warning stickers. These are cheap atlas decals and give the biggest realism gain per cost.
Raise it about 20 mm on the corner castings so a thin contact shadow line appears under the floor.
renderer_notes: Shadowed long side goes near-black navy because there is no bounce light. On a real one, the corrugation would show more mid-tone variation. Not the asset's fault.

summary: A believable five-bar galvanised field gate on a timber post, but it is bare: no latch or closing post, a thin new post, simplified hinges and no galvanising variation.
critique: The silhouette is right for a UK 12 ft five-bar steel gate: five horizontal tube rails, a mid vertical stay and a diagonal brace from the bottom hinge end up to the top at mid span, with a hanging stile and a slam stile. The length looks about 3.6 m and the height about 1.1 m, which is fine. Problems: (1) The hanging post is too thin and too short. It reads as about 150 mm square and only about 1.3 m high, while a real hanging post is 200-250 mm square or round, stands 1.5-1.8 m out of the ground, and has a weathered top (a chamfered or bevelled cap rather than a neat pyramid). (2) It is a perfectly clean, uniform tan colour with no grain, checking cracks, green algae or ground-line darkening. (3) The hinges are small grey blocks. Real gates hang on hook-and-band hinges (a 16-19 mm pin on a through-bolt, with the gate eye wrapping it), and the top one is often adjustable. (4) There is no latch: no spring latch, no chain and hook, no Cotswold latch, and no shutting post with a stop. The free end of the gate hangs in mid-air, which is unrealistic for a static asset. (5) There are no top-rail end caps, no top-rail being a larger tube (normally the top rail is about 42 mm and the lower rails about 25 mm), and no tube-joint weld beads. (6) The galvanising is a single dark-to-silver colour depending on lighting. It needs dull spangled zinc (metallic, roughness about 0.5-0.6) with white rust and darker oxidisation patches.
suggestions: Add a shutting post (same section as the hanging post) at the free end with a spring-loaded or Cotswold latch, plus a chain and hook. Cheap (about 300 tris), and it immediately makes the gate read as installed.

Hanging post: 225 mm square, 1.6-1.7 m above ground, a simple 30-45 degree single-bevel or weathered top, with 4-6 mm chamfers on the edges. Use a weathered oak/tanalised pine material: albedo about 0.25-0.3, darker toward the ground, vertical grain normal map, end-checking cracks on the top, and a green algae tint on the north side.
Hinges: model hook-and-band hinges, with a through-bolt and nut on the far side of the post and a 20 mm pin, and a gate eye collar around the stile. About 150 tris each.
Top rail: make it about 1.6x the diameter of the lower rails. Add plastic end caps on the stiles and small weld fillets at the rail-stile joints (normal map or tiny rings).

Galvanised material: metallic 1.0, base 0.55-0.62 grey, roughness 0.45-0.65 modulated by a spangle noise. Darken the lower rails with mud splash, and add patchy white zinc oxide. Optional painted variants (green, red oxide).
Add a mud-and-wear patch on the ground under the swing arc and a slightly drooping free end (2-3 degrees sag) as optional variation.
renderer_notes: The gate tubes alias at distance and look much darker in back-lit views because of the lack of ambient specular. Treat this as a renderer limitation.

summary: Correct 205 L drum shape with two rolling hoops and bungs, but it is a clean single-colour cylinder: no chimes, no lid detail, no labels, no wear.
critique: The proportions are close to a 205 L steel drum (about 585 mm diameter x 880 mm), with two rolling hoops and two bungs on the lid. However, the top and bottom lack a proper chime, the 15-20 mm rolled seam lip that projects above the lid and gives drums their characteristic rim highlight. Here the lid looks nearly flush, with only a thin edge. The rolling hoops are thin, symmetrical rings. Real ones are pressed outward beads about 25-30 mm wide with a concave groove either side, and the body between them often has subtle swage corrugation. The bungs are low grey discs. They should be a 2 in and a 3/4 in threaded fitting with a raised flange and a cap. The material is one clean satin blue with no metallic edges, no paint chips at the chimes and hoops (where drums get rolled), no rust, no drips, no stencil, hazard diamond or label. The cylinder segmentation is visible on the close-up (faceting on the hoops), and the side seam weld line is missing. Even as a cheap prop this reads as a CG blockout.
suggestions: Chimes: extend the shell 20 mm above the lid and below the base, and roll it into a 12 mm-wide torus lip at both ends. This gives the key highlight. About 200 tris.

Rolling hoops: make each a raised 25 mm bead with a small concave groove either side (3-ring profile), placed at 1/3 and 2/3 height. Optionally add 2-3 shallow swage rings between them via the normal map.
Lid: recess it 15 mm below the chime, and model the two bungs with raised flanges (Ø 70 mm and Ø 40 mm) and cap tabs. Add a faint radial pressed ring on the lid.

Material: paint albedo about 0.05-0.12 linear for the blue (the current value looks too light and saturated in places), roughness 0.45-0.6. Add edge wear on the chimes and hoops exposing metallic steel (metallic mask), rust streaks running down from the top chime, oily drips and grime on the lower third. Use a 1K atlas for the drum family plus per-instance colour (blue, red, black, green, yellow).
Decals: a hazard diamond, a white stencilled UN code or product name, and a weathered paper label patch. 2-3 swappable decal variants.
Add a vertical side weld seam (a narrow normal-map line), and raise the cylinder to 32 sides at LOD0 so the hoops stop faceting on close-up. Add a dented variant via vertex offset.
renderer_notes: The bottom view shows the drum floating slightly with no contact shadow. Check whether the base sits at y=0 or whether this is a shadow bias issue.

summary: Placeholder-level: a faceted white disc on a pole, a cube LNB on a stick and loose ballast blocks. The construction doesn't match any real dish.
critique: The form is meant as a non-penetrating roof-mount (ballast frame) dish, roughly 1.8-2.4 m. Issues: (1) The reflector is a low-poly faceted ellipse with visible polygon edges on the rim, and no rolled rim, no back ribs and no thickness detail. (2) The LNB is a grey cube on a single thin rod sticking out of the centre of the dish. Real dishes either use an offset feed arm coming up from the bottom edge (offset dishes) or a prime-focus quadripod or tripod of 3-4 struts from the rim. The LNB and feedhorn is a cylinder with a conical scalar ring, not a cube. (3) The mount is a single thin pole joining the back of the dish with no az/el mount head, no elevation adjustment strut, no clamp brackets and no back frame. (4) The ballast frame is a flat grey slab with four loose concrete slabs placed on top. Real non-penetrating mounts are a welded galvanised channel frame (about 1.5-2.5 m square) with diagonal braces from the mast to the frame corners, with ballast blocks sitting in trays on the frame rails. (5) There is no cable running from the LNB down the arm and mast. (6) The materials are flat white, flat dark grey and flat concrete, with no weathering, bolts or manufacturer label.
suggestions: Reflector: use a 32-48 segment parabolic dish of real depth (f/D about 0.6), with a 30 mm rolled rim and a 2-3 mm thickness shown at the edge. On the back, add 4-6 radial stamped ribs and a central back plate. About 1.5k tris.

Feed: replace the cube-on-stick with an offset feed arm (a 40 x 40 mm square tube) from the lower rim up to an LNB holder. Model the LNB as a 50 mm cylinder plus a feedhorn cone with scalar rings (about 200 tris). For a larger prime-focus dish, use a 3-strut tripod from the rim instead.

Mount: add an az/el head (a 120 mm pipe clamp plus an elevation hinge plate) and an elevation adjustment threaded rod, mounted on a 76-90 mm galvanised mast. Add 2-4 diagonal braces from mid-mast to the frame corners.

Ballast frame: make it an open galvanised channel frame (100 x 50 mm C-sections) in a square with cross members, with standard 440 x 215 x 100 mm concrete paving blocks stacked 2-3 high in the corner trays. Add a rubber protection mat under the frame.

Add a black coax cable (8 mm) with a drip loop from the LNB along the arm and down the mast. Add UV-faded off-white paint on the dish (albedo 0.7, roughness 0.5) with dirt streaks from the rim, and galvanised metal (metallic, roughness 0.5) for the mount.
Add a manufacturer sticker on the back of the reflector or the arm and a few bolt heads at the clamp. Cheap decals and small cylinders.
renderer_notes: The bright side of the dish washes out to pure white, which may be exposure plus a too-bright albedo. Keep albedo at or below 0.75.

summary: Placeholder: a flat red panel between two plain poles, with a pixel-font 'TRAINING GROUND' and an unfinished, unfixed back face.
critique: The layout (two posts, rectangular panel, title plus a white sub-strip) is a sensible site entrance sign. Execution is greybox level. (1) The text uses a blocky bitmap/pixel font at low resolution. Real signs use a clean sans (Transport, Arial, Helvetica, or the club's typeface) with crisp edges, and the small strip text is illegible noise. (2) The back of the panel is a flat salmon-pink slab with no colour match to the front, no tray-sign return edges, no rails or channel and no fixing clips. Real signs are aluminium composite or folded tray panels fixed to the posts with banded clips, Zed-clips or Unistrut channel rails on the back. (3) The panel sits in front of the posts with no visible fixing at all and floats. (4) The posts are plain dark-grey cylinders with no caps, no galvanising or powder-coat character, and no base detail (no ground-socket collar, concrete bed or grass wear). Real posts are 76 mm galvanised or powder-coated with domed plastic caps. (5) There is no club crest, no arrows or directions, no reflective sheeting, no weathering and no bird lime. (6) Proportions: the panel is about 1.6 x 1.0 m on posts about 2.2 m tall, which is plausible, but the panel bottom is at about 1.1 m with nothing below it, so the composition looks off.
suggestions: Replace the bitmap text with a high-resolution SDF or vector-rendered sans-serif texture (at least 1024 px wide for the panel). Use a real hierarchy: club crest at the left, 'TRAINING GROUND' in bold caps, a sub-strip with 'Reception · Parking · Pitches' plus arrows in a legible size.

Panel construction: model it as a tray sign, a 3 mm face with 25 mm folded returns, rounded corners (r 20 mm) and a 6 mm white or silver border. The back should be bare brushed aluminium (metallic, roughness 0.4), not pink.
Fixings: add 2 horizontal channel rails on the back (40 x 20 mm) plus 4 banded post clips (each a 6 mm-wide ring around the post with a bolt block). About 300 tris.
Posts: 76 mm diameter, black powder-coat (albedo 0.04, roughness 0.45) or galvanised, with domed caps (12 mm high). Add a slight dirt band at the base and a small worn soil/grass ring.
Weathering: subtle UV fade on the red (shift toward pink-orange at the top edge), dirt streaks from the top edge, and a sticker or graffiti tag as an optional variant decal.
Optional: add a thin retroreflective film effect (raised specular) for headlight readability.
renderer_notes: The back face appears pink because of lighting on a lighter red albedo. Even so, real sign backs are bare metal, so this is an asset issue.

summary: A small covered terrace-to-seat stand with bench rows; plausible massing but clean, repetitive and undetailed.
critique: The stand has believable small-ground massing: about 8-10 rows of green seating on a concrete rake, a covered roof and an open front. However, the seats read as continuous green bars rather than individual tip-up seats or benches with legs. There are no aisles with steps and handrails, no front crush barrier or perimeter wall, no row or seat numbering, and no vomitory or access stair. The concrete rake is clean light grey with no staining. The end walls are plain sheared brown slabs that look unfinished. For a Sunday league or non-league ground, the stand is also overbuilt relative to typical 100-300 seat stands, which are often prefabricated modular (e.g. Arena Seating) steel units.
suggestions: Instance individual seats (about 60 tris per seat at LOD0, collapsed to bars at LOD2) or explicit benches with legs. Add 1-2 aisles with 90 mm step risers and galvanised handrails.
Add a 1.1 m front wall or barrier with a painted coping, and side cladding panels (profiled steel sheet or block wall) on the end walls instead of plain brown planes.
Weather the rake: water staining at the riser edges, gum and dirt on treads, faded seat colours varying by row.
For the Sunday league preset, offer a prefabricated modular steel stand (3-5 rows, raised on steel legs, with cladding) as the variant, which better matches real grassroots grounds.
renderer_notes: The interior under the roof is lit only by flat ambient, so seat rows lose contrast. AO would help, but the seat geometry is the main issue.

summary: A simple lattice-truss mono-pitch roof on green columns; reads correctly but is thin and clean, and has an odd scaffold gantry poking through it.
critique: The front lattice truss and green circular columns are a reasonable small-ground roof. However, the roof sheet is a flat untextured plane with no profiled sheeting, no gutter or fascia, no downpipes and no purlins visible from below. The rafters are dark lines. The columns have no base plates or bolts. The camera or scaffold gantry sits on top of or through the roof as a free-standing grey frame with no ladder or access and no platform guardrails that tie it into the structure, so it reads as a floating object. The roof's back edge meets the rear wall without a flashing.
suggestions: Apply a profiled steel sheeting normal map (32 mm trapezoidal, 200 mm pitch) to the roof underside and top, and add a 150 mm fascia and gutter along the front with 2-3 downpipes down the columns.
Add base plates (400 x 400 mm with 4 bolt heads) to the columns and visible purlins (Z-sections every 1.5 m) under the roof.
Seat the camera gantry on the roof structure, or move it to the stand front at roof level with a caged access ladder and guardrails. Otherwise remove it from the Sunday league preset.
Add a translucent roof-light strip or two and slight rust streaks below the gutter.

summary: The stand's ends and rear are flat brown wedge-shaped slabs; there is effectively no facade.
critique: From the side views the stand's end wall is a single uniform brown triangular plane with no material detail, openings, cladding, signage, turnstile or entrance. Behind it the site is an empty paved plaza with a lone concrete post. For a real non-league ground, the exterior would show block or brick walls, profiled steel cladding, a turnstile block, a clubhouse, fencing and gates, rubbish bins and a club crest. Even at small scale, this reads as an unfinished blockout.
suggestions: Clad the rear and end walls with a material set: fair-faced blockwork (normal-mapped, 440 x 215 mm module), or a profiled steel sheet in club green with a 1 m brick plinth. Add drainage staining.
Add an entrance: a turnstile hut (prefab, about 2.5 x 2 x 2.6 m) with a 'PAY HERE' sign, a palisade or weldmesh perimeter fence with gates, and a crest sign on the stand back.
Populate the plaza with existing kit props (bins, benches, lighting columns, a container used as a store) to break up the empty paving.
Remove or justify the lone vertical concrete post at the stand corner (it reads as a stray object).

summary: Tall tapered masts with 4-lamp headframes read correctly at distance, but the heads are tiny and undetailed.
critique: The column heights (about 15-18 m relative to the stand) and the tapering are plausible for a non-league ground, and at night they produce believable pools of light. Up close, the headframes are just small bars with 3-4 flat boxes. There is no lamp bracket frame, lamp hoods or visors, aiming knuckles, control gear box, access ladder or cage, or base door and flange. The masts are plain grey cylinders with no hinge-base or base-plate detail, no galvanised variation and no cable gland.
suggestions: Head: model a galvanised headframe (2-3 m wide, 2 rows) with 4-8 LED floodlight fittings, each about 600 x 400 x 100 mm with fins, on visible knuckle brackets aimed down at the pitch. About 1.5k tris.
Mast: add a base flange with 8 bolt nuts and a small access door at 1 m. Optional: a raise-and-lower hinged-mast pivot or a ladder with cage for older grounds.
Galvanised material with darker streaks below the head. Add a control box at the base.
Make sure lights appear visibly emissive on the fittings at night (the night view shows mostly light pools, not glowing lamps).
renderer_notes: The night shot works as lighting. The issue is the head geometry.

summary: The pitch is the strongest part: mowing stripes, white markings and worn bald patches. Goals and nets aren't legible in this sheet.
critique: The stripe pattern and the worn sandy patches in the goalmouth and along the touchline are a good touch for grassroots realism. However, the lines are perfectly crisp, uniform-width white with no paint fade or grass-through. The stripes are hard-edged blocks rather than soft roller lay. The worn patches look like decals with soft borders rather than churned mud with low grass and footprints. A corner flag is visible. The goals could not be assessed at this camera distance. From the night view they look small, with no clear net volume. The pitch surround is flat green with no hardstanding path, pitch rail or barrier, which a non-league ground (FA ground grading) requires.
suggestions: Soften mowing stripes with a low-frequency gradient and directional sheen, and vary them per stripe. Add grass-through noise and slight fade to line paint (albedo about 0.75 rather than pure white).
Worn areas: blend in a mud material (dark brown, wet roughness 0.3) with sparse grass and a height or normal map, concentrated in the goalmouth and centre circle.
Add a pitch-surround post-and-rail barrier (1.1 m, white or galvanised tube) and a 1.5 m hard-standing path, both required features at stepped-up non-league grounds.
Show goals in at least one detail view so nets can be judged.
renderer_notes: Detail view 2 is badly framed (mostly sky and paving), so a lot of information is lost. Re-frame it toward a goal.

summary: Clear glazed dugouts with green roofs and benches read correctly, but are clean and simplified; no tunnel is visible.
critique: The dugouts are a sensible clear-polycarbonate shelter type with a green-trimmed roof and a bench inside, sitting at the halfway line. However, the frame members are thin uniform boxes, the polycarbonate is perfectly clean with no scratches, dirt or reflections, and there are no individual seats or bucket seats, technical area markings, kit bags, bottles, water cooler or step. There is no players' tunnel or retractable walkway visible linking the stand to the pitch.
suggestions: Add individual moulded bucket seats (instanced) and a floor plinth step, plus a painted white technical area box in front of each dugout (1 m either side, 1 m in front).
Polycarbonate: add roughness and dirt variation at the bottom edges, a faint scratch normal, and a tinted edge. Add a club crest decal on the back panel.
Add a retractable tunnel or a gap in the stand front with a gated players' entrance between the dugouts.
Add small props (water bottles, kit bag, cones) as optional dressing.

summary: Perimeter boards with crisp, plausible local-sponsor graphics are the most convincing element, but they are pristine and simple.
critique: The boards have convincing local-business sponsors (J. Hargreaves & Son, Lumen Sport, Bridge St Garage) with clean typography and taglines, and a believable angled freestanding A-frame placement. To lift them: the boards are perfectly clean and unwarped, with uniform colour, no fixing bolts, no frame edges and no rust or dirt splash at the base. At a grassroots ground, boards are usually fixed to the pitch-surround rail as flat PVC banners or aluminium panels, often of slightly mismatched sizes and ages, with fading and peeling. All the boards share the same exact height and lighting response. No scoreboard is visible (fine for this tier).
suggestions: Add per-board variation: slightly different heights (800-1000 mm) and lengths, UV fade on older boards, and a couple of PVC banners with eyelets and cable ties on the rail.
Add a visible frame edge or back support legs (box section A-frame) and mud splash on the lower 150 mm.
Add subtle panel seams every 2-3 m and a few fixing screw heads.
Mix in a hand-painted or faded sign (e.g. an old plywood board) for grassroots character.

summary: Decent leaf-card canopy with dappled shadows, but the form is a low blob on a short, thin trunk; it doesn't read as a mature English oak.
critique: The leaf cards give convincing, broken foliage texture and dappled shadows, which is good. The structure is wrong for Quercus robur. (1) The trunk is short and thin relative to the crown: it looks like a 1.5-2 m clear stem at about 0.3-0.4 m diameter under a crown about 8-10 m wide, while a mature oak has a 0.8-1.5 m trunk, first branches at 3-6 m, H 20-35 m and spread 15-25 m. It reads as a young ornamental tree or a shrub. (2) The crown is a dense rounded blob with no visible scaffold limbs, no gaps or sky holes, and no characteristic oak shape: broad, irregular, with heavy horizontal or tortuous main limbs and clumped, layered foliage masses separated by gaps. (3) The foliage colour is uniform bright mid-green with no darker interior, no seasonal variation and no yellow-green highlights at the top. Oak leaves are deeper and more olive. (4) The trunk has no buttress flare at the base, no fissured bark detail, and no root flare into the grass. (5) There are no visible branches inside the canopy, even in the top view.
suggestions: Rescale and restructure: trunk diameter 0.9-1.2 m with buttress flare to 1.5x at the ground, clear stem 3-4 m, then 3-5 heavy scaffold limbs radiating at 40-70 degrees, some near-horizontal, with tortuous kinks. Total H about 18-22 m, spread about 18 m. About 3-5k tris for the branch mesh at LOD0.
Build the canopy as 6-12 distinct foliage clumps placed at the limb ends, with gaps between them so that sky and limbs show through. Avoid a single ellipsoid volume.

Leaf material: shift the albedo to an olive-green (about sRGB 70,95,45), add per-card hue and value variation, darker inner cards (AO baked by depth into the crown), and translucency/subsurface for back-lit leaves. Use a lobed oak leaf alpha texture rather than generic leaves.
Bark: a deep fissured bark normal map (tiling 1-2 m) with grey-brown albedo about 0.15-0.2, plus moss on the north side and base.
LOD: crossed billboards or an impostor for distance. A 1.5k-tri LOD1 with clumps as cards keeps it instanceable by the hundred.
renderer_notes: Sun-only shading with flat ambient makes the canopy interior read too bright. Real trees have a much darker core, so AO baked into vertex colours would help.
